text:
Help me write a cover letter. I've taught high school chemistry for 9 years and I'm applying to be a training coordinator at a pharmaceutical manufacturing plant about 30 minutes from me.

About me:
- I teach about 140 students a year across five classes.
- I wrote our school's lab safety program in 2019. Since then we've had no injuries in our labs that needed more than first aid.
- Our AP Chemistry pass rate went from 41% to 58% over the four years I've taught the course.
- Every year I train our new science teachers on lab procedures, about 12 hours each. There have been two a year on average.
- I've never worked in a regulated industry. The job posting asks for experience with GMP training records, which I don't have.
- I use Google Classroom. The plant uses a learning management system I haven't used.

I want the letter to say I can cut their new-hire training time in half. One page.

Before I draft, a few questions. The answers will change what the letter says.

1. **What is the "cut training time in half" claim based on?** Do you know how long their new-hire training takes now, or have you cut training time somewhere before? For example, did your 12-hour onboarding for new teachers replace something longer? A hiring manager will expect a number like that to be backed up. Without a basis, it could hurt you, because it suggests you don't yet understand what makes GMP training long (much of it is required by regulators). If you have no basis, I'd suggest a claim you can support, such as making their training stick better or run more efficiently. But tell me what you have.
2. **What are the company name, the job title as posted, and the hiring manager's name if you know it?** And besides GMP training records, what are the top two or three things the posting asks for?
3. **What records does your lab safety program keep?** Think sign-off sheets, safety quizzes students must pass before lab work, chemical inventories, incident logs, or audits. Any of these would be the closest thing you have to GMP training documentation, and I'd use it to address that gap directly.
4. **Have you learned other platforms quickly**, like a gradebook system, a district LMS before Google Classroom, or lab software? And have you taken or started any GMP or regulated-industry training? Even a short online course would help.
5. **Why this move, and why this plant?** One honest sentence is enough, for example "I want to train adults where the stakes are higher" or "I want to stay in the area."

If you don't know an answer, just say so. I'll write around it and won't guess.

1. I don't know how long their training takes now. But when I rewrote our new-teacher lab training in 2020, it went from 20 hours to 12. If I can't back up the "half" claim, I'm fine with saying what I did at the school instead.

2. Calder Pharmaceuticals, the plant in Westfield. The title is training coordinator. The posting names Karen Doyle as the HR manager. I don't have other top requirements to give you beyond the GMP training records.

3. I keep a signed training record for every new teacher I train and for every student's lab safety quiz. The state has audited our lab safety records twice and found nothing.

4. I don't have other platforms to mention. I've enrolled in an online GMP basics course that finishes May 2.

5. I don't have much beyond it being about 30 minutes from me.

I left out the "cut it in half" claim. You don't know Calder's current training time, and part of GMP training length is set by regulators, so a promise like that would invite doubt. What you actually did is stronger: you cut your new-teacher training from 20 hours to 12, which is 40%. The letter uses that.

[Your Name]
[Address] · [Phone] · [Email]

[Date]

Karen Doyle
HR Manager
Calder Pharmaceuticals
Westfield, [State]

Dear Ms. Doyle,

I am applying for the Training Coordinator position at Calder Pharmaceuticals' Westfield plant. I have taught high school chemistry for nine years. Much of that work has been what a training coordinator does: designing safety training, delivering it, documenting it and checking that it worked.

In 2019 I wrote my school's lab safety program. Since then, no one in our labs has had an injury that needed more than first aid. The program keeps a signed record for every student's lab safety quiz and for every new teacher I train. The state has audited those records twice and found nothing. I know GMP training records are a different standard, and I won't pretend I've already met it. I have enrolled in an online GMP basics course that finishes in May. I also already have the habit the role depends on: no one does the work until their training is complete and documented.

I also train our new science teachers on lab procedures, about two a year. In 2020 I rebuilt that training and cut it from 20 hours to 12. I kept the content that mattered and dropped what didn't. I'd bring the same approach to Calder's onboarding. I would learn what each part of the training is there to do, keep everything that's required and make the rest faster and easier to retain.

Teaching 140 students a year has taught me to explain technical material to people who start at very different levels, and to measure whether they actually learned it. Over the four years I have taught AP Chemistry, our pass rate rose from 41% to 58%.

My classes run on Google Classroom, and I haven't used Calder's learning management system yet. I expect to learn it quickly, and I'll be ready to keep accurate records in it from the start. I live about 30 minutes from Westfield.

I would welcome the chance to talk about how I can support your training program. Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]
</final_document>

Before you send it:
- **Date the course.** "Finishes in May" assumes May 2027. Use the full date if that reads better to you.
- **Add a reason for the move.** The letter has none beyond the short commute. If you have one, even "I want to train adults in work where the stakes are high," add it to the last paragraph. Hiring managers who see a career change often wonder why.
